examples.title: DO NOT BUY FROM NETGEAR - HORRIBLE SERVICE!!!!
examples.text: DO NOT BUY FROM NETGEAR! Horrible customer service - worse than horrible!  This router worked fine for about 4 months.  Then it died suddenly.  After checking out settings, etc., I was pretty certain that the problem was with the hardware.  Called customer service only to find that they only will offer free support for 3 months, though the hardware is warranteed for 1 year.  But they wouldn't even speak to me about the hardware issue until I paid the $100 support fee. And they kept telling me that since the lights were on that it couldnt' be a hardware issue.  So I paid the $100.  Then the nightmare started.  I ended up having to call them about 30 times over the course of a month. The technicians knew less than I do about computers, and they didn't have me do anything that I hadn't already done (except spend a lot of time reinstalling and rebooting). I swear I almost had a heart attack dealing with them.  They barely speak English, transfer you a million times, don't follow through on what they say, etc.  Even worse, they won't look at or don't keep a record of previous transactions, so every time you call or are transferred, you have to tell your entire story all over again.  I have never been rude to customer service people over the phone before, but I ended up screaming and swearing at these people.  Even when they said they would replace the router, they would not send me the information I needed to actually get it without many more phone calls.  Then, I told them I wanted my support fee refunded since it was a hardware issue and under warranty.  That was a million more phone calls, and still it appeared on my credit card report.  So back to the phone and explaining everything from the beginning since they refuse to read the records.  Maddening.  I pray that this one doesn't break, but if it does, I will throw it out and buy another brand.  Oh, and the ability to use the second frequency is pretty useless since there are few devices out there that support it.  Stay away from this Netgear product and any other!

examples.product_title: TomTom GO 930 4.3-Inch Widescreen Bluetooth Portable GPS Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
examples.title: Don't be foolish like me: Buy a Garmin. PLEASE.  Tech support is SO bad.
examples.text:
Some months have gone by and I feel I can give an assessment based on experience of using the unit AND using their tech support & customer support. Mine is a 920 but essentially the same as a 930. Important thing is they're made by the same company, which is unbelievable bad with customer support.

This is the fifth GPS navigator I have owned, my first TomTom.

With most consumer electronics products the after-sale support is only important when something goes wrong; with GPS units it's also critical even when the item is functioning correctly. Mainly because of map and technical updates and the complicated nature of these feature-loaded units like the 920 or 930.

The other reviews have give lots of info on the technical aspects of TomTom devices, so I'll just say that it works reasonably well if you don't expect to use features like voice-entry and bluetooth syncing with your cell phone. I would give it a 3 out of 5 for operational performance.
It's the customer support that really brings down the score: it's horrible! First, it takes many, many days to get an answer via email. Forget about toll-free phone assistance: you'll miss at least one meal waiting for someone to answer your call.

My 920 package included a fancy certificate with computer-generated code (called "Always up to Date") that purportedly represented one year free map updates of the maps that came with your unit. That's what the certificate said, and it gave instructions how to obtain these. Problem was, it didn't work, so this initiated many email requests for technical assistance from me. First they said I had to fax them my receipt, even though this model was introduced less than a year ago and the guarantee is for one year.
Okay, once that was done, the Activation Code on my certificate was apparently inoperable and the 1-year guarantee it clearly stated turned out to be 30 days. And the maps it guaranteed? only North America, not all the maps (namely, Europe) like the certificate promised.

By the time all the delayed emails had been sorted out, my 30 days was up and I was out of luck. Too late to return it to the vendor, too.

Everywhere I asked for advice while shopping for this GPS I was consistently told "Buy Garmin" !! Foolishly I ignored this advice and now I'm stuck with a so-so unit that has one-year-old maps.

Don't make my mistake; Please !! Buy Garmin

(unless you live overseas, in which case I'm told the customer service is better, since that's where the company originated and is based. The North American market is just an after-thought for them; they don't even offer a Mexico map, like Garmin and the other companies.)

examples.product_title: Razer Mamba Rechargeable Wireless PC Gaming Mouse (2012)
examples.title: Worst Mouse Ever?
examples.text:
The mouse is an overpriced desk weight, constantly UN-docks from pc when in wireless mode (freezing and crashing), its average at best in on wired mode, often freezing midway through a task, requiring it to be turned on and off, before working again.

The ergonomics are not what they are made out to be, the only way the rubber grips on the side are of any use is if you hold the mouse in a position that will surely lead to carpel tunnel.

This mouse also requires "special" software called "synapse 2.0" to run its features,
the mouse actually works better when you UN-install the software, but then of course you lose all the features, like variable DPI etc (the rare times the mouse is working).

Battery life on wireless mode is nothing like the 16 hours claimed, and even with the ability to "program" a low battery warning it often dies without warning, forcing you to remove the dock and plug into the wired mode.

Support form the company is hopeless.

Basically if your after a reliable product, dont buy this or any other razor mambo products.

This mouse has so much raw potential, however its been left as unrealized potential, not even worth it at a 10th of the price.

I hate this so much I think I'll end up doing a review on you-tube smashing the hell out of it with a hammer!

Save your money and frustration and buy something else

examples.product_title: 2-Year Protection Plan plus Accident Coverage for Kindle Fire (Previous Generation)
examples.title: NOT 5 Star Customer Service
examples.text:
I bought a 2 year ADH coverage warranty for my Kindle Fire because my warranty experience with claiming my Kindle Keyboard went so smoothly. In that case I was sent an Amazon giftcard (with a little extra back!) for the full investment of my 2 year old Kindle Keyboard. It was almost enough money to upgrade to the Kindle Fire which I was thrilled about! The value of the Kindle Keyboard had dropped significantly with the Fire's release, but I had no worries because I got my full investment back.

The same warranty for the Fire was more expensive at $50 but I thought for sure it'd be worth it. I was so very wrong. When the sad day came that my Kindle Fire went for a swim, I called their helpline to start the claim process. Apparently the warranty for the Kindle Fire and the Kindle Keyboard are owned by different companies, despite both bearing the Squaretrade name. Giftcard payout was not an option. I was disappointed because I had actually wanted to get a Kindle Paperwhite now that I have a smartphone that can do everything the original Fire can. I was told that was not an option, which I totally understood, despite feeling that it was possible however unorthodox. I was still happy because according to the warranty contract "In some cases, we may send you a newer version." I assumed this was their purported 5 star service coming in to action! A newer version of my product has been released equaling the original value of my Kindle Fire. Despite talking to a supervisor, this was not "possible". It's just "not something that we can do". Language like that really bothers me. If they truly wanted to make a customer happy, they could CHOOSE to do the right thing and return my full investment in the form of the Kindle Fire HD.

I find it hilarious that they flat out "don't have access" to a Kindle Fire HD or Kindle Paperwhite so that I could either get my full investment or the cheaper product that I truly want. Again, this is where I feel that it is not that they cannot help me, but that they do not want to help me. Apologies aside, they lost a customer when I was told that my replacement kindle would be refurbished. So not only did I lose $40 in value of my product by them not replacing the full value of my original investment, I'm losing an additional $30 which is how much less the refurbished Kindle Fires cost. I spent $50 on this warranty to lose $70 in the end. How does that make sense? How is this "protecting my investment?" I understand that my original request for a Kindle Paperwhite was unorthodox, but is it WRONG of me to ask for the newer version of the product I protected through them? It IS in their contract that that is an option. However it is clear that they will save money wherever possible by sending out refurbished units until they are not available. It's not like I'm asking for a more expensive version. More importantly, how in the hell did I get a full return of my investment from the very same company 1 year ago? I kept hearing that I'm trying to "upgrade" when I talked to the manager. That sure does sound like I'm trying to pull one over on them huh? Sure feels the other way around!

I understand that they have policies, but they are so vague in the contract so that they can twist it whichever way can save/make them the most money. Well guess what Squaretrade? You can count me out for a warranty on my next e-reader. What I'm likely to end up doing is selling the refurbished (used) Kindle Fire for a fraction of what I originally paid so that I could just get the actual product that I want! I'd be saving them money if they sent me the Paperwhite that I actually want.

Oh, best part? I just got an email stating "Please note that, as set out in our returns instructions, you need to return the original item within 30 days of the date of this e-mail. If you do not return the original item to us within 30 days, we reserve the right to charge an amount equal to the price of your original Kindle order to the payment card you used for the order." So if I didn't send back my nonfunctional Kindle, Amazon would charge me the FULL $200 I originally paid for the Kindle Fire. The refurbished model they're sending me is worth $70 less. So essentially, because I made the mistake of buying a warranty from Square Trade, they reserve the right to rip me off $70 if I don't return a broken Kindle. I get that new stuff comes out and prices go down but if I'm not allowed to expect the full value of my Kindle, who are they to do the very same? Don't they have enough of my money? Talk about adding insult to injury.

In summary, this company has the potential to be just like the rest of them if you expect them to follow through with their misleading promises. Your best bet to TRULY protect your FULL investment is to get a waterproof case and never drop it.

examples.product_title: Garmin Edge 1040 GPS Bike Computer | 2022 Cycling GPS Computer with VO2 Max, Maps, & Multi-GNSS | Cycle Bundle with PlayBetter Tempered Glass Screen, Black Silicone Case, & Tether
examples.title: Who let this come to the market?
examples.text:
Well, this is a fantastic device, in theory.

It is relatively big and that may, or may not, suit you. It comes with different accessories to mount it. No complaint there.

It has all the features promo material did mention. Some are more useful, some make you wonder why you would ever need them. It promises to cover virtually anything you may want to have, check, or follow. Truly a versatile machine.

And then there is usability of it all.

As another reviewer mentioned, getting around menus and figuring things out is a chore. Along the way, you may find out that the command you would like to have is missing.

For example, you cannot delete recent searches. They keep on piling up until your Garmin decides it is enough and then it will delete older ones. Sure, you might have not wanted to delete that particular old one, but it will go. Instead of it, you may end up being left with more recent ones you do not want anymore. There are threads on the Internet discussing this peculiarity, even on Garmin's own forum.

There are three physical buttons. One on the side (on/off, etc.) is just fine. The other two are at the bottom edge. They are a bit firm and you push up, you do not press down. It is a little awkward, to say the least. You will need them, though. Once you figure out what they can consistently do.

By now, you are likely used to cellphone screen. This is not it. This screen has MS-DOS vibe to it. Sharpness was not considered during the design. It is also not that bright. Even with brightness set to the highest level, it is anything but bright. Thankfully, once you increase brightness over certain level, Edge 1030 Plus will warn you that it will shorten the battery time so you should lower it. Screen has lots of glare even on a cloudy day. On top of already not-so-sharp and not-so-bright screen. Touch responsiveness can be adjusted, but even on the most responsive setting it is not that precise.

It is a GPS machine after all so you may try to find a route. Route calculation is slow, but you hopefully have time. In fact, if your destination is far (whatever that means, but 200 miles qualifies), it will give you warning that it will take a long time to calculate and that you should pick some closer "via" point. How will you know where your "via" point may be if you do not know what route/roads you will be taking?
Acquiring satellites is an interesting exercise. For example, today it took more than 20 minutes to find them. After that, the building was apparently moving at 2-3 km/h for a minute, or two. Maybe it would have continued moving more, but satellites were lost. During the time Edge 1030 Plus sat on the window sill, that window moved 200 meters, or so. At least that is what Edge was showing.

Eventually, your route may be calculated. Directions are relatively small letters on top of the screen with map under them. Even in the least busy option (you can adjust amount of details) map is somewhat busy looking. Arrow/cursor is very small (no way to adjust that) and it blends with the road. Why there is no option for simple navigation on the screen is beyond me. Just one large arrow with clear indicator of what is coming next and number for distance would do wonders. Many cars have it. Here, you get that as one small line on top of the 3.5" (dim) screen. Hopefully, you will not be riding in the traffic so you will be able to focus on the screen. Simply because there are no spoken instructions. There is a beep of sorts. That is all. You hear it before it is too late, or you miss it. There is a rumor, and I have not checked it, that you can hear spoken instructions through earphones if you have Android phone connected. Which effectively increases the price of this Edge 1030 Plus by whatever the price of your phone was. Hopefully, you are not riding anywhere near traffic. Earphones while riding are not the best recommendation for such moments. Instead, you can try to decipher the screen. While looking ahead. Again, I just heard that spoken guidance is available in that setting, but I have not confirmed it myself.

There is an "automobile" option for routing. Trying to find the route between two of the major USA cities ends up as "not routable on the map" (or something to that effect). At that point, you get the suggestion on your GPS navigator to opt for "direct" (again, maybe not exact words but to some effect of that). That will draw you a nice straight line from point A to point B. Not that you bought this to use in the car, but just an illustration of how it works. Good for your next helicopter flight.

Battery lasts 24 hours, that is what promo material says. I do not doubt it does last that long, as long as you do not turn the Edge 1030 Plus on. In more real-life situation I just used 10% in about 45 minutes on the street. It included one route calculation and screen brightness at higher (not the highest) setting to enable me to see anything through the glare. And glare there is.

What you are left with is a great device with lots of functions that are a little convoluted to figure out and that will be displayed on the screen that has miserable resolution and is not bright even when on the setting when it drains the battery fast. Your GPS route will take time to calculate and your guidance will be by listening for a beep and reading the screen while you are trying to focus on the road. Once you get home, you will check all the graphs, statistics and what not and hopefully enjoy that.

I have not tried using it with multiple optional sensors, or $1200 pedals to measure the power, but based on experience with more basic things, I would not trust those numbers for a second. I am not saying they are not reliable, but if GPS capability is iffy...

Strongly discouraged to buy as a GPS navigator. In fact, really, who put this out and why are we buying it?

A newer version of my product has been released equaling the original value of my Kindle Fire. Despite talking to a supervisor, this was not "possible". It's just "not something that we can do". Language like that really bothers me. If they truly wanted to make a customer happy, they could CHOOSE to do the right thing and return my full investment in the form of the Kindle Fire HD.

I find it hilarious that they flat out "don't have access" to a Kindle Fire HD or Kindle Paperwhite so that I could either get my full investment or the cheaper product that I truly want. Again, this is where I feel that it is not that they cannot help me, but that they do not want to help me. Apologies aside, they lost a customer when I was told that my replacement kindle would be refurbished. So not only did I lose $40 in value of my product by them not replacing the full value of my original investment, I'm losing an additional $30 which is how much less the refurbished Kindle Fires cost. I spent $50 on this warranty to lose $70 in the end. How does that make sense? How is this "protecting my investment?" I understand that my original request for a Kindle Paperwhite was unorthodox, but is it WRONG of me to ask for the newer version of the product I protected through them? It IS in their contract that that is an option. However it is clear that they will save money wherever possible by sending out refurbished units until they are not available. It's not like I'm asking for a more expensive version. More importantly, how in the hell did I get a full return of my investment from the very same company 1 year ago? I kept hearing that I'm trying to "upgrade" when I talked to the manager. That sure does sound like I'm trying to pull one over on them huh? Sure feels the other way around!

I understand that they have policies, but they are so vague in the contract so that they can twist it whichever way can save/make them the most money. Well guess what Squaretrade? You can count me out for a warranty on my next e-reader. What I'm likely to end up doing is selling the refurbished (used) Kindle Fire for a fraction of what I originally paid so that I could just get the actual product that I want! I'd be saving them money if they sent me the Paperwhite that I actually want.

Oh, best part? I just got an email stating "Please note that, as set out in our returns instructions, you need to return the original item within 30 days of the date of this e-mail. If you do not return the original item to us within 30 days, we reserve the right to charge an amount equal to the price of your original Kindle order to the payment card you used for the order." So if I didn't send back my nonfunctional Kindle, Amazon would charge me the FULL $200 I originally paid for the Kindle Fire. The refurbished model they're sending me is worth $70 less. So essentially, because I made the mistake of buying a warranty from Square Trade, they reserve the right to rip me off $70 if I don't return a broken Kindle. I get that new stuff comes out and prices go down but if I'm not allowed to expect the full value of my Kindle, who are they to do the very same? Don't they have enough of my money? Talk about adding insult to injury.

In summary, this company has the potential to be just like the rest of them if you expect them to follow through with their misleading promises. Your best bet to TRULY protect your FULL investment is to get a waterproof case and never drop it.

examples.product_title: Garmin Edge 1030 Plus, GPS Cycling/Bike Computer, On-Device Workout Suggestions, ClimbPro Pacing Guidance and More
examples.title: Who let this come out to the market?
examples.text:
I have posted this review in "Edge with some extras" first, but I think prospective buyers should be aware of a few things.

Well, this is a fantastic device, in theory.

It is relatively big and that may, or may not, suit you. It comes with different accessories to mount it. No complaint there.

It has all the features promo material did mention. Some are more useful, some make you wonder why you would ever need them. It promises to cover virtually anything you may want to have, check, or follow. Truly a versatile machine.

And then there is usability of it all.

As another reviewer mentioned, getting around menus and figuring things out is a chore. Along the way, you may find out that the command you would like to have is missing.

For example, you cannot delete recent searches. They keep on piling up until your Garmin decides it is enough and then it will delete older ones. Sure, you might have not wanted to delete that particular old one, but it will go. Instead of it, you may end up being left with more recent ones you do not want anymore. There are threads on the Internet discussing this peculiarity, even on Garmin's own forum.

There are three physical buttons. One on the side (on/off, etc.) is just fine. The other two are at the bottom edge. They are a bit firm and you push up, you do not press down. It is a little awkward, to say the least. You will need them, though. Once you figure out what they can consistently do.

By now, you are likely used to cellphone screen. This is not it. This screen has MS-DOS vibe to it. Sharpness was not considered during the design. It is also not that bright. Even with brightness set to the highest level, it is anything but bright. Thankfully, once you increase brightness over certain level, Edge 1030 Plus will warn you that it will shorten the battery time so you should lower it. Screen has lots of glare even on a cloudy day. On top of already not-so-sharp and not-so-bright screen. Touch responsiveness can be adjusted, but even on the most responsive setting it is not that precise.

It is a GPS machine after all so you may try to find a route. Route calculation is slow, but you hopefully have time. In fact, if your destination is far (whatever that means, but 200 miles qualifies), it will give you warning that it will take a long time to calculate and that you should pick some closer "via" point. How will you know where your "via" point may be if you do not know what route/roads you will be taking?
Acquiring satellites is an interesting exercise. For example, today it took more than 20 minutes to find them. After that, the building was apparently moving at 2-3 km/h for a minute, or two. Maybe it would have continued moving more, but satellites were lost. During the time Edge 1030 Plus sat on the window sill, that window moved 200 meters, or so. At least that is what Edge was showing.

Eventually, your route may be calculated. Directions are relatively small letters on top of the screen with map under them. Even in the least busy option (you can adjust amount of details) map is somewhat busy looking. Arrow/cursor is very small (no way to adjust that) and it blends with the road. Why there is no option for simple navigation on the screen is beyond me. Just one large arrow with clear indicator of what is coming next and number for distance would do wonders. Many cars have it. Here, you get that as one small line on top of the 3.5" (dim) screen. Hopefully, you will not be riding in the traffic so you will be able to focus on the screen. Simply because there are no spoken instructions. There is a beep of sorts. That is all. You hear it before it is too late, or you miss it. There is a rumor, and I have not checked it, that you can hear spoken instructions through earphones if you have Android phone connected. Which effectively increases the price of this Edge 1030 Plus by whatever the price of your phone was. Hopefully, you are not riding anywhere near traffic. Earphones while riding are not the best recommendation for such moments. Instead, you can try to decipher the screen. While looking ahead. Again, I just heard that spoken guidance is available in that setting, but I have not confirmed it myself.

There is an option to be reminded to eat, or drink. Now, this may be the first GPS device ever not to include POI (points of interest). You will be in unfamiliar area (that is why you need GPS) and it will tell you to go and have a drink and you will need to orient yourself by luck to imagine where something of interest might be. Of course, you may have your water bottle with you, but you will have to guess the direction you would be able to refill it in. Basically, you need to know where you are going and what is around so you can put coordinates in. Google it first and pretend that Google Maps do not exist. Makes a GPS device a little less useful.

There is an "automobile" option for routing. Trying to find the route between two of the major USA cities ends up as "not routable on the map" (or something to that effect). At that point, you get the suggestion on your GPS navigator to opt for "direct" (again, maybe not exact words but to some effect of that). That will draw you a nice straight line from point A to point B. Good for your next helicopter flight.

Battery lasts 24 hours, that is what promo material says. I do not doubt it does last that long, as long as you do not turn the Edge 1030 Plus on. In more real-life situation I just used 10% in about 45 minutes on the street. It included one route calculation and screen brightness at higher (not the highest) setting to enable me to see anything through the glare. And glare there is.

What you are left with is a great device with lots of functions that are a little convoluted to figure out and that will be displayed on the screen that has miserable resolution and is not bright even when on the setting when it drains the battery fast. Your GPS route will take time to calculate and your guidance will be by listening for a beep and reading the screen while you are trying to focus on the road. Once you get home, you will check all the graphs, statistics and what not and hopefully enjoy that.

I have not tried using it with multiple optional sensors, or $1200 pedals to measure the power, but based on experience with more basic things, I would not trust those numbers for a second. I am not saying they are not reliable, but if GPS capability is iffy...

Strongly discouraged to buy as a GPS navigator. In fact, really, who put this out and why are we buying it?

examples.product_title: SOLIOM Security Camera Outdoor Wireless Battery Powered,1080P WiFi Indoor Home System with IP67 Waterproof,Night Vision,2-Way Audio,Siren Alarm,Motion Sensor,Schedulable Working Time B06
examples.title: For the price there is better out there than this...
examples.text:
It is rare I write bad reviews, however when it is a product that deserves a bad review this is it. There are some major flaws that unfortunately this camera has some great potential and works great when it is working. If you want to have 30 days cloud photos and video from movements captured be ready to spend $39.99 per camera per year. We have five cameras so that is $199.95yearly which I don’t mind covering if they would work properly.

I purchased (3) of the Soliom Wireless wifi S600s, and (2) of the Soliom S800 outdoor wireless security camera has a built-in 14400mAh rechargeable battery over the past 6 months. I say this so you know that this is not based on a random order of one camera but off of two different versions and five total cameras from the same company.

Pros:
1- The night vision and picture quality is very good, and clear to see details.

2- S800 battery: When it works it is worry free on a cloudy day (battery lasts only 2-3 weeks), where the camera S600 with only the recharging solar panel lasts only 2 days without sun.

3- The Spotlight: is very strong and lights up the front yard which makes an intruder think twice.

4- Cloud Service offered: Once you pay the 39.99 per year to connect there is 30 days of video and photos you can look back to retrieve or download.

5- SD Data Storage slot available: Up to 64 GB of a micro SD card can be added (not included) to capture if you do not want to pay for the Cloud service however to see the videos you will need to go up to your camera, retrieve the SD card and look at the videos through your computer.

CONs:
1- “FREE Gifts”? In each of the camera boxes (5) we received a card for a free SD card or a 6 month Cloud membership free. All we had to do was text a number and provide the order number. WRONG. We were told to leave a positive review and take a picture and send to them and we would receive a free gift. Since I am not the type of person to be bought to write a positive review for something “Free” I told them that I would not be writing a review until after 4-6 months of use of the camera and that I would leave an honest review. After about 2 weeks of texting back and forth on if there was a free gift and choosing, and not receiving, and being told by them to leave a positive review again and they would send the free gift I stopped writing them. NEVER GOT THE FREE GIFT, AND WILL NOT BE BOUGHT TO WRITE A POSITIVE REVIEW. So I wonder how many “positive” reviews on this are due to getting the free gift…..

2- Initial Setup: This camera is sluggish and slow to setup, connect to the wifi (we have highspeed with points outside), and the barcode works but takes FOREVER to setup. Took about 25-30ish min to setup.

3- Connecting Camera after battery dies: Once the battery dies, you will need to go through the process again to add the camera… barcode… entering the wifi and naming…. ALL of IT as it was a new camera EVERY TIME IT IS TURNED OFF.

4- Battery life: on the S800 lasted from a fully charged battery for ONLY 2 weeks. It advertises that it will last up to three months… not true. Both cameras were dead within 2-3 weeks in the month of August in Utah. So it was not hot summer, and not cold winter that ran it out. It was poor quality batteries. The S600 with solar panels died in 2 days when there was a cloudy day so I had to climb the ladder and recharge the solar panel and then RE-SETUP THE CAMERA by following the initial setup and installing again. When we had a storm for 1 week I had to do that every 2 days so 3 total until the sun came through the clouds enough to recharge the camera battery.

5- There is a pinkish glow livestream when the device is charging via solar, the pink tinge exitst only when the panels are charging. Cheap DC to DC converter? Perhaps. Other reviewers have also commented on this, so it is not only our observation.

6- You CANNOT SAVE videos from the app that are stored on the SD card without physically removing the card from the device.

7- No way to verify the account once you register: You are forced to create an account to log on. After there is no verification that it is registered.

8- Construction of the camera: The housing is thin plastic which probably won’t survive a 4’ drop. The lens, infrared and the LED lights are also all plastic.

9- Motion detection is random: At times a leaf will send a warning and record, and another with a person standing in front dancing will produce no warning or recording.

10- Won’t work /or setup if not connected to the internet: We have a backup for when the electricity goes out, however without an actual connection to the internet THIS WILL NOT WORK. Even if it is connected to our wifi etc. I searched through the other reviews and saw others having the same issue. So when lights go out and the “bad-guys” search for places to break in… you are OUT OF LUCK with this camera. Isn’t this why we purchased the cameras for?

examples.title: Constantly Getting Under-Voltage Warnings from My Raspberry Pi 2
examples.text:
Encouraged by a positive review, I purchased this DC converter module for my Raspberry Pi 2 project. Based on my hands-on experience, I can assure you that this module consistently provides the border line voltage around at 4.65V throughout booting and up in the idle mode. You will see under voltage warnings wallpapering the console screen along with a tiny yellow lightning sign coming on and off constantly at the top right corner of the display. Yes, this is inadequate for your Raspberry Pi 2 and up.

It can freeze up or even power down your Raspberry Pi any time, potentially damaging the file system, especially when you try to do any computing of your own. For sure, there can be many applications this module would be perfect for where it can be rated 5 stars. But using it with Raspberry Pi 2 and up is definitely not one of them.

examples.title: Useless When You Need It
examples.text:
Samsung really dropped the ball on their SmartTag products -- they are HORRIBLY UNRELIABLE!!!

Finding your SmartTag is something you hope you never actually need to do because it means you've lost something. Unfortunately, if you rely on Samsung SmartTags, you will never find it. That's because the device is poorly supported. The battery WILL die on the tag and you WILL NOT KNOW until you try to find a lost item.

It would have been very easy for Samsung to ALERT you when the battery is getting weak, but it DOES NOT. So, when you try to find your tag, you'll realize that the battery has died and it is no longer tracking -- USELESS!!!

The hardware might be okay, but the software is unfriendly, complex, and poorly designed.

Maybe Apple's tags are better -- I will find out.

examples.product_title: Edifier G2000 32W PC Gaming Computer Speakers for Laptop Mac Desktop Computer Woofer Speakers Bluetooth USB 3.5mm AUX Inputs RGB Lights Multimedia Speakers Black
examples.title: There are much much better options
examples.text:
I got tired of reading endless forums about the "best budget desktop speakers" so I decided to purchase the following and compare them in real life against each other: Neumi BS5P | Micca PB42X | Klipsch ProMedia 2.1 THX | Edifier R1280T | Bose Companion 2 Series III | Edifier G2000.

I am not an audiophile, I am not technical. I have played instruments my whole life and run sound in some amateur settings, so I'm guessing I have a slightly more critical ear than the average listener, but definitely not of those truly dedicated to hi fidelity listening. I don't know proper terms. I took these notes kind of haphazardly, but they are listed in order of best to worst after personal testing. I intend to play games and listen to music with a slight preference towards gaming as I have another speaker system for music that I can use for music.

High level takeaway: the true battle is between the Neumi BS5P and the Micca PB42X. Between those 2 speakers, either would be the right choice of all these options depending on your intended use. I ended up choosing the Neumi because I am going to be playing games quite a bit, and they provided much better low end to fill out a lot of the sound effects. If I were choosing a speaker just for music listening, I would have gone with the Miccas as they have superior mid/high/vocal clarity. The Miccas have a good enough sub that I wouldn't be missing the low end on most music, but if I wanted to, I could just add a sub to fill out the lows on the Miccas (for edm type music).

_______________________________________________________________________________________________

Neumi BS5P 75-Watt $139.99 - My personal winner
Pro:
- Sounds full and satisfying right away
- Great bass (almost as good as the dedicated sub on the Klipsch, definitely better than all other options without a dedicated sub. I've got adjacent neighbors so I won't ever go sub heavy anyways, so don't need a dedicated sub with the power these pull)
- Decently clear mids/highs, though this is less defined than the Miccas. These get better after doing the firmware update, and get it much closer to the Micca's clarity, but still not quite as good
- Bluetooth pairing quality stays really high (doesn't make a difference for me)
Cons
- Mids/highs/vocals still just not as good/clear/crisp as the Micca
- Much larger than the other options (might be a pro if you're looking to fill a room with more volume - I'm not looking for that)
- Need to update the firmware to get better mids/highs than out of the box (minor inconvenience but might scare some away)

Micca PB42X $109.99
Pro:
- Really nice, crisp/clean mid/highs (better than everything else) The vocals are bright and shiny, unrivaled by any other of these options
- Doesn't seem to add much coloration (but this also leads to it feeling slightly emptier than the 1280T, could be good or bad)
- Pretty good bass for what it is (far better than the G2000 and Bose, worse than the others)
- It comes with a 2 part dc cable that's longer than others, and a longer mp3 cable than others (doesn't really matter, but it's nice)
- Fairly flat (might be a good or bad thing for usage)
Con:
- Getting really nit picky just to find differences, but the connection cable on the back is a twisty, rather than a poke as the Edifiers have. Twistys just seem less stable/more exposed
- Mids/lows start to sound more tinny in comparison to the mids/lows of the neumi, leaving a somewhat less satisfying feeling
- Ultimately this feels a bit emptier than others with better subs, but is also definitely crisper/clearer

Klipsch ProMedia 2.1 THX Certified $144.99
Pro:
- Great sound out of the box
- Great bass (only one with a dedicated sub, so that should be obvious)
Con:
- Decent mid/highs, but still not as crisp/clear as the Miccas

Edifier R1280T $129.32
Pro:
- Beautiful aesthetic
- Good sound out of the box , there's not the obvious tinny sound of budget speaker
- Volume, bass, and treble knobs
- I'm satisfied with the sound immediately (I grew less satisfied with the sound the more I A/B compared to the Bose due to the coloration. I then adjusted the tilt of the speakers and it seemed to fix this coloration issue and bring more clarity to the mids/highs)
- It's really minor, but the power plug is a plug and not a brick like all the others
Con:
- No sub out option
- Definitely colors the sound to fill in the space more (which could be a pro for some people too). Ends up adding a layer of mud to the overall sound
- The mids/highs are really just muddy due to the coloration

Bose Companion 2 Series III $149.00
Pro:
- The mids/highs are nice and bright and clear
- Really compact if you don't have a lot of desk space00
- I'm satisfied with this sound out of the box
- Seems not to color the sound (certainly not nearly like the R1280T), feels more accurate
- Has an upward tilt so it seems to naturally position for the sweet spot
Con:
- Only a volume knob so no automatic control over bass/treble (I assume there's eq software that would fix this?)
- Bass is a bit lacking (probably would be satisfied with the amount of bass if I weren't comparing against the others)
- Something feels emptier about these speakers against the 1280T and Micca

Edifier G2000 $109.99
Pro:
- Decent bass and presence
- The LED light is kind of nice
Con:
- Stupid startup car sound is absolutely childish and obnoxious
- The LED light stays on (I think you can turn it off but who's going to go through the hassle of turning it off and on if you have to hear the stupid car sound at every startup)
- Still clearly sounds like a budget speaker with a constant of tin/noise
- Bass can wash out pretty easily at medium volumes
- It crackles at other certain sounds like my incoming email ping
- Not satisfied with this sound out of the box

First, let me say that I typically steer clear of anything with the Monster Cable brand on it because I feel it is overpriced. That's why I was surprised to find this 500ft spool of 14ga cable for such a reasonable price.

Last year I used this cable to wire a surround system in my family room and it has worked perfectly. The cable is very flexible and has a marking for every 1' of length, so it's easy to tell how much you've pulled. (The mark isn't just a tick, it actually has the number of feet printed.) It has a low-friction shielding so it's easy to pull and an internal rip-cord helps remove the shielding when you're tying this into speakers.

This is 14ga wire, which was perfect for my usage. Anything smaller starts to impact sound quality on longer runs, and larger wire is a pain to work with for some connectors and speakers.

Overall, I would highly recommend this cable. To me, this strikes a perfect balance between price and performance.

examples.product_title: Alpine SWR-1223D 12" Dual 2 ohm Type-R Subwoofer
examples.title: All the hype you've heard? It's true!
examples.text:
Let's keep this simple. My "best bang for the buck" system (in a Scion XB):
Panasonic HU, Polk Audio DB401 4" in the dash, Polk Audio DB651 6.5" in the doors.
MTX TE801D (800 watts @ 2-ohms mono bridged, underrated), 2 Alpine Type R SWR-1223D 2-ohm DVC (wired at 2-ohms mono), these 2 Atrend E12Sv B Box Series boxes, stuffed with 1 pound of Polyfill each, as suggested. I bought these boxes to replace the tiny sealed boxes I had these subs in before.

Both boxes fit perfectly in the back of my Scion, I have them facing upwards. Mind you, I haven't broken the subs in fully (I've played them for only a few hours). I installed the subs into the boxes today, hooked them up, and went for a little drive. Mother of G*d.

Let's backtrack a little. Prior to purchasing the Alpines, I had 2 MTX 8000s in the same tiny sealed boxes. I had stuffed those with about 3/4 of a pound of Polyfill. Now, the 8000s sounded decent in those boxes, but I felt it wasn't loud enough for my liking, but enough for the average listener. So I purchased the Alpines, noticed an improvement in both sound quality and sound pressure level (loudness). Even though they were in boxes that might've been too small, I felt the stuffing them made quite a difference. Bass was very tight and punchy. It was plenty loud, but again, after everything I'v read about these subs, I knew ported was the way to go. And so I ordered the Atrend boxes. And man.... what a HUGE difference.

Nevermind those stupid YouTube videos about how the subs make the body of the car flex. My car is a Scion XB, a toaster. Cheaply built. I could probably burp loud enough to make the car flex. And for whatever reason, the right rear panel flexes so bad you can hear it in the cabin, loud enough that some notes may sound like distortion. In other words, those videos really don't mean much.

Now, let me tell you about my 15 minute drive. I drove to a local shopping center parking lot, and cranked up Jay-Z and Kanye's "Welcome to The Jungle" from the "Watch The Throne" album. Maybe it was just coincidence, but a car alarm went off, about 20 feet away from where I was parked. My doors and windows were closed.

Drove off, drove by a local dog park, had the windows down, cranked DJ Laz's "Can U Feel It?" (you need to download this song NOW), was driving about 40 mph and managed to set a car's alarm off that was parked about 4 lanes away ON THE OPPOSITE SIDE OF THE ROAD! That's impressive to me.

Anyway, for someone who doesn't have time to wait for custom boxes or installations, this has been the perfect solution for me. These subs in these boxes provide probably more than enough bass for me. I'm talking about the bass is so loud, any more bass could qualify me for some kind of SPL competition (not what I'm looking to do). Honestly, I could get away with half this system and be satisfied. If you're looking for the perfect sub/box combo, look no further! *One last tip, the prices on these boxes fluctuate almost daily. I purchased mine from this seller for $31.92 + $15.62 each for shipping. Keep this in mind when buying. Any questions, please feel free to ask, and give a thumbs up if I've helped with my review :)

examples.product_title: Tamrac 3447 Rally 7 Camera/Laptop Bag (Black)
examples.title: Great bag, a bit too big for my use
examples.text:
I purchased both the [[ASIN:B0045O0DHW Tamrac 3445 Rally 5 Camera/Netbook/iPad Bag (Brown/Tan)]] and [[ASIN:B0046SB5L0 Tamrac 3447 Rally 7 Camera/Laptop Bag (Brown/Tan)]] bags as I was looking for a daily use camera bag. I had a few key criteria for what the bag had to hold:

1. Be able to hold my camera ( [[ASIN:B001EQ4BVI Canon EOS 50D]] )
2. 1 flash ( [[ASIN:B0002XQWCK Canon Speedlite 580EX]] or [[ASIN:B001CCAISE Canon Speedlite 430EX II]] )
3. 1 lens on Camera and at least 1 additional lens
4. [[ASIN:B002C7481G Apple iPad]] in this case: [[ASIN:B0042X8XBY Twelve South BookBook for iPad in Classic Black Style]]
5. Assorted: memory cards, ipad camera kit, charger (iPad and camera), spare battery, etc.
6. Place to keep a water bottle or 2

The Rally 7 bag has 4 vertical compartments, whereas the Rally 5 has 3 vertical compartments. Both bags have a compartment for keeping a laptop, netbook or tablet. In addition there are 2 mesh pockets on either side, a zippered compartment at the front of the bag (under the flap) and a document pocket in the back of the bag.

The Rally 7 held everything great, I could hold All of the above comfortably. I could fit my [[ASIN:B00007GQLS Canon EF 100-400mm f4.5-5.6L]] lens and 2-3 other lenses, depending on which ones I used. The problem was exactly what I could fit in the bag. Since this is going to be my walking around bag (and what I carry to work every day) I needed to keep myself from over filling the bag. The space for the iPad was plenty large and could easily hold a laptop instead (up to 15"). The pockets on the sides of the bag are pretty nice for keeping small items or water bottles and the front pocket under the flap holds all the assorted accessories I need.

The Rally 5 on the other hand basically has one less slot so I can hold everything that I listed above, but the 100-400L lens. The iPad slot fits my iPad in case just barely or could fit a netbook instead (up to maybe a 11" or 12" screen, my 13" MacBook does not fit). The bag is a little shorter and not quite as wide as the Rally 7, but the depth of the bags is just about the same as can be seen in the photos i have added to the bag pages or in the specs provided by Tamrac. The best part is that the bag now goes with me wherever I go, so I take more photos. I have to plan things more carefully than I did with my backpack, but at the same time this makes the bag lighter.

I ended up returning the Rally 7 and kept the Rally 5. I'm not sure either of these bags could hold a Pro body or a body with a grip, but since that isn't what I have it wasn't a concern. Here are a few things that I would like done differently on the bag:

1. Add the quiet opening velcro flaps like on the Crumpler bags (that I also looked at, but were too heavy).
2. Allow the strap to be changed, although the strap is reasonably comfortable, I can see wanting a different strap or one with more padding.
3. I'm not sure I like the clip in the front for closing the flap, it doesn't have the guides on the side which means I don't quite get it lined up all the time.

Other than those 3 items I really like my new bag! I've been using it for almost 6 weeks now and have found it to be exactly what I needed and when my camera isn't it, I can even use it to hold the 100-400 lens to shoot with at an event so I can get at it and swap lenses. I like the brown color as well (though I did like the black bag with red stripe that was available for other versions of this bag, that didn't have the laptop/iPad slot).

Note: I've posted this review on both the Rally 5 and Rally 7 pages as I hope this helps anyone trying to decide between these bags.

examples.product_title: IDMAX 12D2 V.3 Image Dynamics 12" Dual 2 Ohm Voice Coil 1000 Watts RMS Subwoofer
examples.title: Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2 and comparison to Alpine SWR-1242D
examples.text:
The Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2 is truly and amazing sounding subwoofer with good power handling. The effect I was looking for was "shock and awe", and I have found mostly what I am looking for in this subwoofer. I have a rear folding seat that separates the trunk from the cabin. After some positioning experimentation, I have decided that it sounds best firing the sub and port forward directly into the cabin (and sealing the trunk from excessive sound with memory foam packed firm at the sides of the box. Very smooth and musical and hard hitting bass from the very low notes from around 20Hz all the way up to the crossover point (I am using 80Hz). Let me say that almost no one that has heard this sub can believe that it is only one 12" sub. Even sales pros and an SPL competitor (his setup gets to 154dB) who have heard this setup made these kind of comments; one person said they expected to see 2 15's and at least a thousand more watts....most were surprised to see only one 12. My review mirror is tight, yet it will move the full range of motion (about 3 inches) is just a couple seconds on some tracks. If I would have this enclosed in the trunk, it would likely destroy or loosen tail lights, and I would have ridiculous rattles without significant sound deadening.

Not only is the bass low, strong, and clean, but it is very punchy with the right tracks - one track that has extreme "kick thru the chest" is "I'm So Over You" by Lil Wayne Ft. Shanell.

My previous subwoofer was an Alpine SWR-1242D 12". While the Alpine sub sounds very good, it does not compare to the clean sound and output of the IDMAX 12. I didn't like the Alpine sub facing the cabin. There is a concern for the IDMAX that needs to be addressed - here is a comparison to note:

The Alpine SWR-1242D 12 is rated at 600 watts RMS, 1800 watts peak.

The Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2 is rated at 1000 watts, 1800 peak,

However, the Alpine sub is clearly capable of handling more power than the IDMAX 12;

Within 2 days of owning the Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2, with intense bass tracks such as Bass Zone (Peaks @ 30, 40, @ 50 Hz by Quad Maximus) - at maximum volume levels must have truly heated the voice coil to the point where it warped and started rubbing. The IDMAX voice coil is smaller than most subs competing in the advertised power range of this sub (1000 RMS), and this is part of how the Sensitivity of 93.1 is achieved because there is more cone area when a smaller voice coil is used. The tolerances are also tighter, meaning the voice coil is a little closer to the magnet and components - making this a potential problem. Fortunately, I was able to force the coil back into position in an unconventional - not recommended way...by tapping pretty hard on the side of the sub where I had the most rub. This actually worked somehow and it does not rub anymore at all, even at high volume. Though I have had to repeat this a couple times in the last 6 months as I tend to be an extremist and keep pushing it to the limit. I just have to watch it. I know now that if I can smell the voice coil smoking - I better turn it down for a while - if it already isn't too late! (DUH!)

The Alpine sub seemed a bit "bullet proof" and although I pushed it as just as hard and for much longer time, I had no such issues.

So to recap... it's all pros, except I wish it was more conservatively rated and I wish it could handle a bit more power. This is truly a very loud (93.1 sensitive) sub and makes the most of the power it is fed. Compared to the Alpine sub I had, I have to say the Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2 blows away the Alpine SWR-1242D 12. After owning the two it seems there is no comparison. Keep in mind you should expect this when comparing two subs that are in a completely different price range. It is my opinion that you are probably getting more for your money with the IDMAX than many competing subs out there - even though this is a more expensive sub than most.

So keep in mind that the power handling of the Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2 is accurate, but not conservative, while the power handling of the Alpine SWR-1242D 12 is simply conservative, as it handled more than rated power without showing signs of a problem.

Components used in my system:
* Pioneer AVH-P4300DVD - ($348.00 eBay mid 2011 - nice for the money but really has issues with noise when auto EQ or other equalization settings are used)
* Pioneer CD-BTB200BT - (JUNK - nearly no integration with the AVH-P4300DVD)
* Alpine PDX-M12 & Alpine RUX-KNOB (highly recommended)
* Image Dynamics IDMAX12 V.3 D2 (highly recommended)
* AudioEnhancers TX320 Enclosure (Nice enclosure for the money! Around $110.00)
* Alpine MRP-F300 (recommended but might replace it with the Alpine PDX F4)
* Polk Audio MM691 6x9' pair (nice sound)
* Infinity Reference 6032cf 6.5-Inch pair (these are inexpensive but put out excellent sound for midrange and high frequencies and can handle decent power)(might replace with Polk MM6501 separates)
* Optima Yellow top.
* Tsunami Fbw701-anl fuse holder
* Raptor RANL2502 fuse
* The big 3 with KnuKonceptz.com Kolossus Fleks Kable 1/0 (highly recommended), and some Rockford Fosgate 0 AWG
* Absolute CAP5000 50-Farad 16V Capacitor (for power conditioning only - I wouldn't be surprised if this tested out to be somewhere between 2-4 Farad - I am skeptical - but I somehow got it on Amazon for $65.00, then the next day the price was raised to $160.00 ...at least it has 0 gauge hook ups, looks good and the volt meter is accurate - I know it has some capacitance as it will light a dual filament 12V 8 watt light for about 20 seconds, of which about 14 seconds are bright (so if someone knows the approx. capacitance based on that let me know! Starting voltage with alternator off at 12.9v)
* Monster MPC I304 4C RCA & Monster MPC I302 2C RCA (tight fitting - no noise - Highly recommended)
* Rockford Fosgate RFK4D 4 AWG Dual Amplifier Install Kit (didn't use the RCA's from this kit for too long - they are junk - these were the cause of noise in my system and even signal drop-outs due to loose connections - fixed this completely with the above mentioned Monster RCA's). Then upgraded to the KnuKonceptz.com Kolossus Fleks Kable 1/0 for most of the main wiring. (Highly recommended)

One of my goals for the above system is efficiency. By going with an amplifier that put out more watts without consuming excessive juice, and this subwoofer with higher sensitivity, I have avoided having to upgrade the alternator (it's already a 105 amp alternator) or use an additional battery.

examples.title: The perfect everyday camera bag for me!
examples.text:
I purchased both the [[ASIN:B0045O0DHW Tamrac 3445 Rally 5 Camera/Netbook/iPad Bag (Brown/Tan)]] and [[ASIN:B0046SB5L0 Tamrac 3447 Rally 7 Camera/Laptop Bag (Brown/Tan)]] bags as I was looking for a daily use camera bag. I had a few key criteria for what the bag had to hold:

1. Be able to hold my camera ( [[ASIN:B001EQ4BVI Canon EOS 50D]] )
2. 1 flash ( [[ASIN:B0002XQWCK Canon Speedlite 580EX]] or [[ASIN:B001CCAISE Canon Speedlite 430EX II]] )
3. 1 lens on Camera and at least 1 additional lens
4. [[ASIN:B002C7481G Apple iPad]] in this case: [[ASIN:B0042X8XBY Twelve South BookBook for iPad in Classic Black Style]]
5. Assorted: memory cards, ipad camera kit, charger (iPad and camera), spare battery, etc.
6. Place to keep a water bottle or 2

The Rally 7 bag has 4 vertical compartments, whereas the Rally 5 has 3 vertical compartments. Both bags have a compartment for keeping a laptop, netbook or tablet. In addition there are 2 mesh pockets on either side, a zippered compartment at the front of the bag (under the flap) and a document pocket in the back of the bag.

The Rally 7 held everything great, I could hold All of the above comfortably. I could fit my [[ASIN:B00007GQLS Canon EF 100-400mm f4.5-5.6L]] lens and 2-3 other lenses, depending on which ones I used. The problem was exactly what I could fit in the bag. Since this is going to be my walking around bag (and what I carry to work every day) I needed to keep myself from over filling the bag. The space for the iPad was plenty large and could easily hold a laptop instead (up to 15"). The pockets on the sides of the bag are pretty nice for keeping small items or water bottles and the front pocket under the flap holds all the assorted accessories I need.

The Rally 5 on the other hand basically has one less slot so I can hold everything that I listed above, but the 100-400L lens. The iPad slot fits my iPad in case just barely or could fit a netbook instead (up to maybe a 11" or 12" screen, my 13" MacBook does not fit). The bag is a little shorter and not quite as wide as the Rally 7, but the depth of the bags is just about the same as can be seen in the photos i have added to the bag pages or in the specs provided by Tamrac. The best part is that the bag now goes with me wherever I go, so I take more photos. I have to plan things more carefully than I did with my backpack, but at the same time this makes the bag lighter.

I ended up returning the Rally 7 and kept the Rally 5. I'm not sure either of these bags could hold a Pro body or a body with a grip, but since that isn't what I have it wasn't a concern. Here are a few things that I would like done differently on the bag:

1. Add the quiet opening velcro flaps like on the Crumpler bags (that I also looked at, but were too heavy).
2. Allow the strap to be changed, although the strap is reasonably comfortable, I can see wanting a different strap or one with more padding.
3. I'm not sure I like the clip in the front for closing the flap, it doesn't have the guides on the side which means I don't quite get it lined up all the time.

Other than those 3 items I really like my new bag! I've been using it for almost 6 weeks now and have found it to be exactly what I needed and when my camera isn't it, I can even use it to hold the 100-400 lens to shoot with at an event so I can get at it and swap lenses. I like the brown color as well (though I did like the black bag with red stripe that was available for other versions of this bag, that didn't have the laptop/iPad slot).

Note: I've posted this review on both the Rally 5 and Rally 7 pages as I hope this helps anyone trying to decide between these bags.

examples.product_title: NETGEAR WG511NA Wireless G Pc Card
examples.title: Great for travel
examples.text:
I haven't seen a review yet that really compared options among various wireless adapters so I thought I'd give it a try.

I live in an apartment complex with concrete walls that barely allow for a cell phone signal. The little bit I use the internet I didn't want to pay 60$/month so I bought a Linksys WUSB54G Wireless-G USB Adapter, Netgear WG511 Wireless 802.11g PC Card, and a Hawking WIRELESS G USB NETWORK ADAPTER w. Hi Gain 6db Antenna basically just to make sure I got one that would work.

The worst of the 3 was the Linksys usb adapter. It could pick up weaker signals without having to balance the laptop at a weird angle out the window, but the software which runs it doesn't like weak signals so anything under 50% keeps the thing scanning even after you're connected. which means constant disconnects unless you manually stop the scanner while connected. Even then, it had a frustrating habit of losing the connection.

The Netgear card was much better at holding a signal, although it did require a balancing act and careful angling to get the signal. The software was great. The biggest complaint I had with this is I was dealing with really low signals which slow the internet to a crawl. It would take a few minutes to load yahoo. With better signals the card would be great.

The Hawking usb adapter is by far the best of the bunch. I'm picking up signals I never saw with the other two, and they are coming in with decent percentages. The software couldn't be better. Connection doesn't take minutes like the other two, and the radar dish antenna can be pointed for better signal gain. I haven't had a connection loss once using it, and the internet is running at better than dial up speed (I'm connecting to a 23% signal).

Overall, I'd pick the Netgear card for travel with a laptop due to it's size and portability, but for home use the Hawking usb adapter was head and shoulders above the others.

examples.product_title: Soundmatters foxLv2 aptX Pocket-sized Portable Bluetooth Audiophile Speaker System, Black, Bluetooth
examples.title: Full Range Sound
examples.text:
Just got the FoxLO about a couple of days back. It's connected to the subwoofer out of the FoxL aptX. The sound from the FoxL itself is pretty good and it's one of the best small speakers I've owned and heard including the JBL Flip, NuForce Cube, Small Jambox, Logitech Mobile Boombox, Beats Pill etc.

The combination of the FoxL and FoxLO gives the unit a full bodied sound and rivals the Bose Soundlink II and Logitech s715i in a smaller and lighter package. In fact the sound is as deep as the Bose Soundock Portable, but only cleaner. The advantage also being that you can unhook the FoxL and carry it with you in your pocket.

The lows are flushed out better with the FoxLO and the mids and highs were always the strong point of the FoxL. Rock, Country, Jazz all sound fantastic thru the combo. Piano, Sax, Guitars and Voices sound neutral and natural. Its like having a mini Hifi if you are within a 10ft radius.

Have yet to try out Bluetooth. It's connected thru the 3.5 mm Aux-in and is being fed lossless music. Battery life of the FoxL seems excellent, but still under review. Will update later on Bluetooth and Battery.

There are a few issues which I feel can be ironed out in the future:
1. The FoxL needs to have an auto off function. I don't know if they have sorted this out in the FoxL Dash 7. It would help conserve battery.
2. In bass heavy tracks the FoxL still moves a bit inspite of the anti-slip mat. The Dash 7 hopefully would have resolved this with its dual opposing passive radiaters.
3. The Level adjustments in the FoxLO are a bit fiddly and you need to adjust the level to bring out the best. It distorts if the level is kept too high.
4. The FoxLO operates only thru AC power. The earlier prototype had a USB charging port for the FoxL and other devices. This is now absent from the model being sold. It would have been good if you could charge the FoxL while it was hooked to the FoxLO.

Overall, for the quality of sound, I would give it 4.5 stars. The negatives mentioned knock it back to 4 stars.

examples.product_title: TomTom GO 920 Portable GPS Vehicle Navigator (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
examples.title: Customer Service is TERRIBLE !!  and that's real important with GPS units
examples.text:
Some months have gone by and I feel I can give an assessment based on experience of using the unit AND using their tech support & customer support.

This is the fifth GPS navigator I have owned, my first TomTom.

With most consumer electronics products the after-sale support is only important when something goes wrong; with GPS units it's also critical even when the item is functioning correctly. Mainly because of map and technical updates and the complicated nature of these feature-loaded units like the 920.

The other reviews have give lots of info on the technical aspects of TomTom devices, so I'll just say that it works reasonably well if you don't expect to use features like voice-entry and bluetooth syncing with your cell phone. I would give it a 3 out of 5 for operational performance.
It's the customer support that really brings down the score: it's horrible! First, it takes many, many days to get an answer via email. Forget about toll-free phone assistance: you'll miss at least one meal waiting for someone to answer your call.

My 920 package included a fancy certificate with computer-generated code (called "Always up to Date") that supposedly represented one year free map updates of the maps that came with your unit. That's what the certificate said, and it gave instructions how to obtain these. Problem was, it didn't work, so this initiated many email requests for technical assistance from me. First they said I had to fax them my receipt, even though this model was introduced less than a year ago and the guarantee is for one year. Okay, once that was done, the Activation Code on my certificate was apparently inoperable and the 1-year guarantee it clearly stated turned out to be 30 days. And the maps it guaranteed? only North America, not all the maps (namely, Europe) like the certificate promised.

By the time all the delayed emails had been sorted out, my 30 days was up and I was out of luck. Too late to return it to the vendor, too.

Everywhere I asked for advice while shopping for this GPS I was consistently told "Buy Garmin" !! Foolishly I ignored this advice and now I'm stuck with a so-so unit that has one-year-old maps.

Don't make my mistake; Please !! Buy Garmin

examples.product_title: Beats Solo2 Wireless On-Ear Headphone - Silver
examples.title: Informative and honest review.
examples.text:
These headphones do produce good sound quality. Although not the best in the market, they are decent but the wireless technology is nothing new and lacks anything to be desired. The sleek design helps in its marketing. It easily fits with the visual aesthetic of Apple products. Unfortunately... Their craftsmanship is very poor. While pretty to look at, I find they sit just a bit too snuggly for extended wear. Whether you're an audiophile, gamer or just overall using them to lounge about in; you'll find yourself adjusting them frequently.

Next up is the constant disappointment in physical manufacturing. These headphones are meant to be powerful, compact and sleekly designed. With that said; you had best not fold them as they were designed to do. As with all headphones, wires are still used to connect the power supply to the speakers. Constant bending of the headphones WILL cause the wires to eventually break or become disconnected. At which point (if you're unlucky like me) you'll have to have them replaced and shipped back to the Apple repair center in Sparks, NV. That is a free process if you are still under warranty. (Just as an FYI, I bought mine in February 2015, and had them sent for this very reason in July of the same year just 6 months after purchase.)

The next thing to talk about is battery life. When fully charged the battery will last throughout most of the day (about 12 hours) without needing to charge a second time. Should that fail, you can still use the company supplied 3.5mm headphone conductor plug. Although that seems self-defeating and possibly one major reason of having purchased a set of Beats Solo 2 WIRELESS headphones in the first place... It's still a great back up. I found that there was no difference in audio quality or playback. Actually, if anything, the microphone on the audio jack conductor plug was too sensitive. I found that I easily overlooked that. What isn't easily overlooked is the constant Power Button malfunctions. (You can google this later if you want.) My Beats Solo 2 Wireless headphones had this very problem as well. Another 6 months after receiving my refurbished pair in July 2015 from Apple's repair center in Sparks, NV. You will be required to keep your Beats up to date with the latest Firmware/Software, and possibly have to soft reset them if you have this problem. At which point, if you still cannot turn them on, you will have to send them in.

I cannot stress enough how important it is to make sure that your warranty is kept up to date. If you're asking yourself, "Why?" My answer is this; should you have to have them fixed or replaced (and your warranty runs out just days before the faulty issues arise like mine did) you will be asked to pay a fixers fee BY APPLE for $129! Nearly half the price of the manufactural defected merchandise.

I've learned my lesson, having been through a set of Beats Studio and Beats Solo 2 Wireless headphones. I keep mine in darn near perfect condition and in my honest opinion when it comes accessories such as this... If it requires a secondary extended warranty, don't buy them. Go get a pair of BOSE, same quality (if not better) audio, definitive comfort for extended wear, superior noise cancellation and they will replace them if there is a manufactural defect regardless of how long you've had them. All this and a price point is the same. Just $20 cheaper than that of Beats. I'm no spokesperson, but I really hope I've been able to help you make a wiser decision. Even if you still buy these headphones, you will get good quality sound... Just not a well-crafted piece of technology. Thanks for reading.

~ NiMH

First, let me say that I typically steer clear of anything with the Monster Cable brand on it because I feel it is overpriced. That's why I was surprised to find this 500ft spool of 14ga cable for such a reasonable price.

Last year I used this cable to wire a surround system in my family room and it has worked perfectly. The cable is very flexible and has a marking for every 1' of length, so it's easy to tell how much you've pulled. (The mark isn't just a tick, it actually has the number of feet printed.) It has a low-friction shielding so it's easy to pull and an internal rip-cord helps remove the shielding when you're tying this into speakers.

This is 14ga wire, which was perfect for my usage. Anything smaller starts to impact sound quality on longer runs, and larger wire is a pain to work with for some connectors and speakers.

Overall, I would highly recommend this cable. To me, this strikes a perfect balance between price and performance.

If you miss this place and fast forward to the next part you have to start all over at the beginning of the previous file.

I have tested this against my regular CLIP using the same books and transferred the same way.

I am a loyal Sansa fan; I had 2 Sansa Express's and 2 Sansa Clips, but this new CLIP + is such a disappointment! ALSO library books (DRM) do not play from the added memory chip.

examples.product_title: Chuwi Hi12 12.2'' Windows 10 Ultrabook Tablet PC with Intel Cherry Trail Z8300 Quad-Core CPU 64 Bit 2166 x 1440 Retina Screen 4GB/64GB WiFi HD-Out USB 3.0
examples.title: NICE FEATURES BUT ANOTHER  WOEFULLY SLOW ATOM CPU
examples.text:
The Z8300 is really an Atom processor, not a Cherry Trail. Chuwi is not being honest. Even though it is a 4 core, 64 bit processor, it is ranked at a pitiful 1,481st place, (Yes, that's right: one thousand four hundred eighty-first place), in processing power among CPU’s on PassMark’s website. That translates into the processing power of 16 bit computers back in the late 80’s and early 90’s.

Chuwi is relying on excellent graphics to overcome the dog CPU. But why mix the two extremes like this? In my opinion, even with the graphics, the Atom CPU makes the Hi12 at best a $200 tablet, even with the keyboard. The CPU tanks when you try to run just one program that exercises it.

I bought the tablet for use with a teleprompter and for lectures with PowerPoint. The slides are not created on the Hi12. I bought it for presenting purposes only, and made the error of doing so without taking the time to look at objective stats about the Intel CPU performance. That was a bad mistake. The Hi12 even drops the ball just using it as a presentation platform for PowerPoint. This is light work use.

On the first presentation it became quickly evident that this thing did not even have enough computing power to bring PowerPoint slides up fast enough to stay in sync with my speaking. I ended up repeating myself and stumbling through the whole presentation. It was a disaster. It would be a foolish mistake to ever try to use the Chuwi for work purposes again.

I hope this is just the beta machine it seems to be. Even the USB ports on the keyboard are upside down. Maybe Chuwi will put a better CPU in a production unit designed for doing some real work. But I don't appreciate being a beta tester without being told so.

So I have a $350 toy for the grandkids. This means I regret having bought the tablet. You can get $200 tablets with keyboards all day long that have three times the processing power of the Chuwi. However, Chuwi is not the company that produced the outright garbage. The garbage is the pitiful Intel processor. After all these years, there is still no end to Intel’s gall.
